pride_data.title: Chemical Probing Discovers New Insights into the Native Assembly State of a  Bacterial Microcompartment
pride_data.projectDescription: Microcompartments (BMCs) are widespread in bacteria and are used for a variety of metabolic purposes, including catabolism of host metabolites. A suite of proteins self-assembles into the shell and cargo layers of BMCs. However, the native assembly state of these large complexes remains to be elucidated. Herein, chemical probes were used to discover structural features of a native BMC. While the exterior could be demarcated with fluorophores, the interior was unexpectedly permeable, suggesting the shell layer may be more dynamic than thought. This allowed access to cross-linking chemical probes, which were analyzed for discovery of the protein interactome. These cross-links revealed a complex multivalent network among cargo proteins that contained encapsulation peptides and demonstrated that the shell layer follows discreet rules in its assembly. These results are consistent overall with a model where biomolecular condensation drives interactions of cargo proteins prior to envelopment by shell layer proteins.
pride_data.sampleProcessingProtocol: Xlinking buffer is 25 mM sodium phosphate pH 7.4, 50 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2. Xlinked for 1 hour at RT covered from light. Reaction was quenched by the addition of DTT to 50 mM. Samples were then flash frozen and stored at -20C. Samples were prepared utilizing the S-Trap mini protocol 4.1 detailed at https://protifi.com/pages/protocols.   Add  350  µL  of  binding/wash  buffer  to  the  sample  and  mix. Place  S-Trap  mini  in  a  2  mL  receiver  tube  for  waste flow  through.  Apply sample to S-Trap column.   Centrifuge  the  S-Trap  column  at  4,000  g  for  30 sec  to trap proteins.   Add  400  µL  binding/wash  buffer;  centrifuge  at  4,000  g  for  30 sec.  Repeat  3  times  and  discard  flow  through as  necessary. Centrifuge S-Trap column  at  4,000  g  for  1  min  to  fully  remove  binding/wash  buffer. Transfer  S-Trap  mini  column  to  a  clean  2  mL sample  tube for  the  digestion. Add  125  µL  of  digestion  buffer  containing  protease,  most  commonly  trypsin or  a trypsin/lys-C  mix,  at  a  1:10  weight  to weight (wt:wt)  ratio  into  the  top of  the  S-Trap.  By example,  for  200  µg  of  protein  to  digest,  apply  20  µg of  trypsin dissolved in  125  µL. Incubate for 1 – 2 hrs at 47 °C for trypsin or trypsin/lys-C, or overnight at 37 °C. Preferably use a water bath or stationary thermomixer. Add 80 µL of elution buffer 1 to the S-Trap then centrifuge (4,000 rcf, 1 min). Add 80 µL of elution buffer 2 to the S-Trap then centrifuge (4,000 rcf, 1 min). Add 80 µL of elution buffer 3 to the S-Trap then centrifuge (4,000 rcf, 1 min). This elution assists in recovery of hydrophobic peptides. Other organics may also be used as needed. Pool eluted peptides, dry down and resuspend in 5% ACN, 0.1% Formic.
pride_data.dataProcessingProtocol: Data processing was performed with Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.5.0.400. Full data search was performed using Sequest HT with precursor match tolerance being 10 ppm and fragment mass tolerance being either 0.02 Da or 0.6 Da, dependent on orbitrap or ion trap fragment scan respectivly. Modifications were restricted to the crosslinker, oxidation (M) being a dynamic modifications and acetylation being dynamic on the N-terminus. Catbamidomethylation was set as a static modification on C. Crosslinker search was performed with the XlinkX nodes utilizing the template in Proteome Discoverer. 10 ppm mass tolerance for the precursor ion scan, 20 ppm for FTMS fragment mass tol, and 0.6 Da for the ITMS fragment match. FDR threshold was set to 0.05 FDR. Results were exported and visualized in xiNET.

passages.text: Chemical Probing Provides Insight into the Native Assembly State of a Bacterial Microcompartment
SUMMARY

Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are widespread in bacteria and are used for a variety of metabolic purposes, including catabolism of host metabolites. A suite of proteins self-assembles into the shell and cargo layers of BMCs. However, the native assembly state of these large complexes remains to be elucidated. Herein, chemical probes were used to observe structural features of a native BMC. While the exterior could be demarcated with fluorophores, the interior was unexpectedly permeable, suggesting the shell layer may be more dynamic than thought. This allowed access to cross-linking chemical probes, which were analyzed to uncover the protein interactome. These cross-links revealed a complex multivalent network among cargo proteins that contained encapsulation peptides and demonstrated that the shell layer follows discreet rules in its assembly. These results are consistent overall with a model where biomolecular condensation drives interactions of cargo proteins prior to envelopment by shell layer proteins.
eTOC Blurb

Bacterial microcompartments (BMC) are large organelle-like structures. They contain enzymes for a particular metabolic pathway surrounded by an icosahedral protein shell. The rules governing their assembly have not been fully revealed. In their manuscript, Trettel et al. observe key structural features of a native BMC using chemical probes and crosslinkers.
Graphical Abstract
INTRODUCTION

Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) are proteinaceous organelle-like structures found in a wide range of bacterial phyla. BMCs consist of two organizational domains – the outer protein shell and the encapsulated enzymes within. This mode of segregation from the cytosol is thought to increase metabolic flux through the pathway by concentrating enzymes and recycling cofactors, while also sequestering volatile, yet toxic, aldehyde intermediates and excluding inhibitors. These benefits have encouraged great interest in pursuing BMC-based biotechnology.

While the inner chemistry may differ significantly between different classes of BMCs, all BMCs are thought to rely on a structurally conserved shell as a modular chassis to accommodate this functional plasticity. The protein shells consist of three classes: hexamers (BMC-H), trimers (BMC-T), and pentamers (BMC-P). These ‘plates’ of shell proteins then tessellate in a relatively stoichiometric fashion to produce a complete BMC shell. Each shell protein also exhibits a characteristic concave and convex face. In total, the shell is generally assumed to be a static barrier that separates the inner lumen from the cytosol. The organizing principles of synthetic shells have been described. In these non-native systems, the concave face of each shell protein faces cytosolically, leaving the convex side responsible for interacting with cargo; however, it is unclear if this arrangement is maintained for native BMC.

It is less clear how the inner cargo assembles and organizes. The cargo-shell interactions are thought to be mediated through short helical extensions on the N- or C- termini of cargo proteins dubbed encapsulation peptides (EPs). EPs are thought to work through hydrophobic packing of a conserved motif to shell proteins and perhaps other EPs on other cargo. In carboxysomes, this latter case led to speculation that liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) plays a role in cargo assembly. However, it has yet to be demonstrated for catabolic BMCs. Cargo lacking EPs presumably ‘piggyback with EP-containing cargo proteins. It is unclear exactly how the EPs may interact with shell proteins due to debate regarding the orientation of shell proteins. For example, while the convex face of shell proteins faces inwards in empty shells, some EPs have been demonstrated to interact instead with the C-terminus of BMC-H proteins on their concave surface. Therefore, fundamental features of BMC structural organization remain to be conclusively determined.

These observations complicate the narrative of modularity that researchers find attractive about BMC-based biotechnology. While synthetic encapsulation approaches have been developed, such as the SpyTag-Catcher system and coiled-coil targeting domains, the development of naturally inspired methods has stagnated. As a result, the orientation of the protein shell and cargo protein-protein interactions (PPIs) in native BMCs must be better defined. This knowledge would significantly improve the understanding of both the natural assembly state and the biogenesis pathway of native BMCs.

In this study, we leverage fluorescent chemical tags and protein cross-linkers to gain insight into the native assembly state of the model Pdu BMC system. These data address some of the open questions about native BMC assembly, including the orientation of protein shell. From our data, we also speculate on a fundamental repeating unit of the shell where BMC-H proteins surround BMC-T. We also report numerous cross-links between the shell and cargo, which implicate the BMC-T protein PduB as a hub for these interactions. Our findings also address the organization of the inner lumen, where we find evidence of a disordered, multivalent network between EP-tagged proteins. We find that these data overall are consistent with liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) of cargo proteins. Together, these data provide new clues for the mechanisms of Pdu BMC biogenesis.

By capturing the Pdu PPI network, our results provide a blueprint for the fully assembled Pdu BMC that we believe will apply to other large BMCs and that will help spur new hypotheses on modes of assembly and rational design efforts. The techniques described here can likewise be used to study other large supramolecular assemblies.
RESULTS
Purification of Salmonella enterica Pdu BMC

To work with purified microcompartments in vitro, we sourced S. enterica Typhimurium LT2 Pdu BMCs (Figure 1a) from a strain of E. coli containing the entire cob/cbi and pdu loci under native control. To investigate whether the Pdu BMC form within E. coli, we co-transformed a second plasmid encoding green fluorescent protein (GFP). This particular gfp (encoding GFPP1−18) also included an N-terminal encapsulation peptide (EP) sequence and a C-terminal proteolytic cleavage tag intended to trigger its degradation unless successfully packaged in a BMC. This approach has been used previously to visualize BMCs in vivo. We likewise observed GFP foci within cells that co-expressed the gfpP1−18 gene (Figure 1b, S1b), confirming in vivo formation of Pdu BMC. Pdu BMCs were then purified from cellular lysates as described previously. An assessment of the resulting material by transmission electron microscopy revealed objects of approximately uniform size and morphology (Figure 1c), which were consistent with the typical appearance of microcompartments. When the purified material was analyzed by SDS-PAGE, it resulted in a banding pattern that matched well with the known sizes and abundances of Pdu BMC proteins (Figure 1d). Together, these data show that our purification strategy results in preparation of intact Pdu BMC.
Shell Proteins are More Accessible to Chemical Probes than Inner Cargo

Given that the shell is generally described as a static entity, we assumed it would act as a barrier to relatively large chemicals. To that end, we decided to use fluorophores with a reactive maleimide handle (Alexa Fluor 532 Maleimide, AF532) to selectively conjugate surface accessible thiols. AF532 was added to BMC samples and aliquots were quenched at varying time intervals, with optimization for concentration and the time of incubation. These samples were separated and visualized by SDS-PAGE (Figure 2a, S2a). A sample of BMC that had been denatured prior to incubation with AF532 displayed more bands than native BMC, demonstrating that the native BMCs exhibit inaccessible cysteines, presumably located within the interior of the BMC, which can be exposed by denaturation of the samples. Bands that are likely to correspond to shell proteins PduJ, PduB and PduB’ (a translationally truncated isoform of PduB), labeled quickly at early time points (Figure 2a) and constituted most of the overall fluorescence. Certain individual proteins (BMC-H protein PduA and cargo protein PduL) do not contain cysteine residues and cannot be detected using AF532. For comparison, the major shell proteins PduB and PduB’ have a cysteine on both the concave and convex side, while PduJ only has one on its convex face. These data show proof-in-principle that simple fluorescent chemical probes can be used to qualitatively demarcate solvent-accessible proteins.

While shell proteins exhibited a higher initial share of the total fluorescent labeling, bands that are likely to include interior cargo proteins were also labeled when given enough time (Figure 2a, b). This unexpectedly suggested that, while the probe may preferentially label the exterior, it can also access the inner lumen over time. An example of this effect is seen with the highly abundant cargo protein PduC.

We also found that shell proteins and cargo proteins label at noticeably different rates, where shell proteins labeled quickly and eventually saturate. The fluorescence of each band was quantified as a fraction of the total fluorescence for each time point (Figure 2b, S2b, S2c). This showed that shell proteins lose their share of total fluorescence as they saturate while cargo components continue to label; therefore, the labeling patterns of interior and exterior differ from one another. Denatured samples showed no such bias towards labeling and intact samples that are denatured can fully recapitulate the denatured state, indicating that AF532 is not limiting. We conclude that the native morphology of the BMC limits the dyes’ access to certain - most likely interior - proteins.
Shell and Cargo Components Can be Chemically Differentiated

Our initial results hinted that information about the shell and lumen can be independently captured given the right conditions. Accordingly, we adjusted our labeling strategy to include a second probe. In this new scheme, the first probe reacts with and blocks accessible residues after which the total sample is denatured and the remaining cysteines are reacted with a second fluorescent probe (Figure 2c). We reasoned that this strategy should label exterior-facing proteins with the first probe (AF532) and interior proteins with the second probe (Alexa Fluor 680 Maleimide; AF680), which could then be analyzed and quantified by SDS-PAGE (Figure 2d).. The identity of the probes was interchangeable; we found that AF680 acts similarly to AF532 (Figure S2d). Individual proteins are not observable by one-dimensional SDS-PAGE; therefore, we utilized two-dimensional (2D) PAGE to separate individual protein spots. These proteins were resolved first by isoelectric focusing followed by separation by mass (Figure 2d). The overall spot pattern agreed well with previously published data, albeit with an overall shift to more acidic pI’s, likely due to the conjugated dyes. Regardless, the 2D analysis showed that some proteins were preferentially labeled with the surface accessible first probe and other proteins were preferentially labeled by the second probe. For simplicity, we elected to independently quantify the two labels for specific zones of the gel since shell and cargo components tended to segregate into specific areas. For each zone, we quantified a ratio of red/green signal, which we interpreted as enrichment for either shell (green biased) or cargo (red biased) (Figure 2e). This method found that areas rich in shell proteins (zones 3 and 5) were enriched for green fluorescence relative to areas rich in cargo components (zones 1, 2, and 4). Some spots were excised and subjected to peptide mass fingerprinting, confirming the presence of anticipated proteins within specific zones (Figure S2d, S2e). Together, these data show that exterior and interior proteins can be visually resolved by 2D PAGE.

This dual-label workflow is not restricted to fluorescent chemical handles.(Figure 2f). To test this hypothesis, we reacted native BMC proteins with maleimide-linked biotin and, after denaturing the entire sample, then incubated with plain maleimide. Biotin-bound proteins were then separated using streptavidin-bound agarose beads. Using this order of chemical probes, the agarose-associated proteins appeared to be enriched for shell proteins (Figure 2f, lane A). However, when the order of the chemical probes was reversed, for selective binding of cargo proteins, the enrichment pattern did not appear to be as strong (Figure 2f, lane B). We speculate that the small size of the plain maleimide probe may allow it to diffuse and block thiols faster when used as the first probe. Therefore, this reaction scheme would need to be optimized further to isolate cargo proteins. Regardless, these data show proof-in-principle that inside and outside information can be independently captured using biotin probes.
Fluorescent Labeling Allows for Direct Confocal Imaging of Native BMCs

BMCs are large but still beneath the diffraction limit of light microscopy. Due to this, most direct imaging has relied on TEM to study their morphology (e.g., Figure 1). We speculated that the fluorescently labeled native Pdu BMCs may be directly observable using optical interrogation methods in vitro, akin to single-particle analyses. To test this, we labeled Pdu BMC with or without Alexa Fluor 488 maleimide (AF488) and analyzed them using laser scanning confocal microscopy (Figure 2g). Unsurprisingly, unlabeled BMCs exhibited no background fluorescence. The same holds true for BMCs incubated with AF488 that had been pre-reduced by dithiothreitol (DTT), demonstrating that AF488 does not non-specifically associate. In contrast, BMCs labeled with reactive AF488 could be visualized as small, defined foci under the conditions we tested. The same results were found with AF680. This demonstrates that fluorescent chemical probes can be employed for direct visualization of bacterial BMCs using light microscopy.
The Protein Shell Displays Chemical Permeability

The current line of thought is that BMCs are a closed system that carefully controls the influx and efflux of metabolites. While fluorescent chemical probes exhibited a bias towards reactivity against surface proteins, we were surprised that they appeared to also access the inner lumen. One possibility is that the overall shell structure may be dynamic, allowing the probe to access the interior. To further test this hypothesis, we employed chemical cross-linkers, which we reasoned would reduce dynamics of shell proteins, resulting in an altered fluorescent labeling profile when tagged with AF532. We chose the cross-linker ethylene glycol bis(sulfosuccinimidyl succinate) (sulfo-EGS) since it can be cleaved after the labeling reaction. When sulfo-EGS was varied between 1 to 5 mM, higher concentrations resulted in formation of a band that would not enter the resolving gel (Figure 3a, S3a), indicating successful cross-linking. Cross-linked BMC samples were then incubated with AF532 and aliquots were removed at time intervals. The cross-link was then reversed with hydroxlamine and the resulting mixture was resolved by SDS-PAGE. Band fluorescence was quantified as a ratio of PduB (a major BMC-T shell protein) to either PduC or PduP (major cargo proteins) intensity. We reasoned that this ratio would change if fluorescence reactivity of cargo proteins was reduced by crosslinking at the surface. Consistent with this hypothesis, the labeling ratio was biased towards an increased labeling of PduB relative to either PduC or PduP (Figure 3b and 3c, respectively). From this we speculate that transient cross-linking of the native BMC can reduce permeability of the shell layer.

These data suggest that BMCs may exhibit some permeability. It is possible that this permeability results from general heterogeneity (i.e., cracks) within the shell or from damage incurred during the purification process. However, an alternate hypothesis is that the protein shell itself is intentionally dynamic. This latter hypothesis has been indirectly explored in a prior investigation of purified BMC-H proteins by atomic force microscopy (AFM), which showed that purified BMC-H proteins assemble and disassemble in real-time. To test this, we purified an S93C mutant of the BMC-H protein PduA (Figure S3b) and labeled it with AF532 to act as a reporter (PduA*). The interaction between PduA* and native BMCs was tested by incubating PduA* with purified BMCs for 30 minutes, followed by low-speed centrifugation of the BMCs and resolution of proteins by SDS-PAGE (Figure 3d). PduA* was not recovered when native BMCs were not added at the incubation step (Figure 3d, lane 3). However, PduA* co-pelleted when incubated with native BMCs. Furthermore, PduA* appeared as a new Coomasie-stained band in the pellet proteins due to its modestly increased mass (from a hexahistidine N-terminal tag and conjugation by AF532).

Together, these experiments suggest that permeability of the Pdu BMC is affected by the status of the layer of shell proteins. However, we acknowledge that our current data cannot differentiate between the free exchange of protein subunits within the shell and binding artifacts caused by damaged shell layers. Therefore, we consider this to be an important open question that should be addressed more thoroughly in further experimentation.
BMCs Can Withstand a Wide-Range of Chemical Modifications

To measure the effect of the reagents used in this study on BMC morphology, we turned to dynamic light scattering (DLS). Using this approach, BMC samples could be investigated for changes in size and polydispersity after derivatization (Figure 3e, 3f). We chose to use DLS instead of TEM in order to avoid the morphological distortions that can be introduced during preparation of samples for TEM, as described previously. When measured by DLS, the peak of the distribution of BMCs (142.2 ± 6.3 nm) did not significantly differ from samples that had been reacted with 125 μM AF532 (146.6 ± 6.6 nm). A sample that had been treated with 2% DMSO alone, which was included in the maleimide-fluorophore assays, also closely resembled native BMCs (144.2 ± 2.3 nm). However, BMCs reacted with a commonly used cross-linker bis(sulfosuccinimidyl)suberate (‘BS3’, 5 mM) exhibited a moderate increase in the peak of the BMC distribution (157.7 ± 6.7 nm) and in polydispersity as well. Since this cross-linking reagent reacts with lysine, this apparent increase in mass may result from the greatly increased presence of lysine-conjugated residues. Regardless, we conclude from these data that BMCs can be modified by chemical probes without major disruptions.
Insights into the Pdu BMC Interactome by Cross-linking Coupled to Mass Spectrometry

The results reported herein have established that BMCs are not only permeable to chemical reagents but can also withstand their modifications. Encouraged by this, we wanted to gain a more quantitative insight into the Pdu BMC interactome and turned to cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) in hopes of getting structural information. While a prior in silico investigation has suggested some protein-protein interactions, there is scant experimental data on the lumen PPI network. Herein, we optimized the concentrations and reaction times of three commonly used amine cross-linkers DSBU, BS(PEG)5, and DSSO (Figure S4) prior to analysis by high-resolution tandem mass spectrometry. In total, this resulted in discovery of interactions between 16 different proteins that are described by 230 unique cross-links. We sub-divide these cross-links into 161 cargo-cargo links, 13 cargo-shell links, and 56 shell-shell links (Figure 4a). A full description of the non-redundant cross-links summarized in Figure 4a can be found in Data S1.
EP-Tagged Proteins Favor Cargo-Cargo Interactions

It is critical to understand how the proteins with EPs act in a native context. The current paradigm dictates that EPs can be fused to cargo proteins to guide them to a cognate shell protein partner. Within the Pdu BMC, four proteins (PduDELP) encode for N-terminal EPs. Our analysis revealed that a majority of the cross-links specifically occurred between PduCDELP proteins, with few cross-links for the other cargo proteins (Figure 4b). Note, PduC does not encode for an EP and is likely included in these links due to forming a dimer of trimers with PduDE. A notable exception is the reactivation factor PduG, which is known to interact with the signature complex PduCDE by displacing PduD. Consistent with this, we observed cross-links of PduG to either PduC or PduE, but not PduD (Figure 4b). Another exception is the propionate kinase PduW, which has been proposed to be located outside of the inner lumen. However, we observed cross-links between PduW and the PduCDE complex (Figure S5). Interestingly, propanol dehydrogenase PduQ cross-linked to the opposite side of the PduCDE complex, relative to PduW.

At first glance, it appears that EPs may act as a general aggregation factor to increase the local concentrations of these proteins to one another and increase their likelihood of cross-linking, thus explaining their enrichment for cross-links. To test this, we co-expressed Pdu BMCs with GFPP1−18 (GFP containing the PduP EP, Figure 1d, Figure 4c) to see if it will integrate into this subnetwork. BMCs purified under these conditions do include GFPP1−18 and, perhaps consequently, a reduced quantity of PduP (red arrow, Figure 4c). XL-MS confirmed that GFPP1−18 incorporated into the EP subnetwork and was captured in cross-links to both PduP and PduL, including cross-links directly between EPs (asterisks, Figure 4b). Note, the N-terminus of GFPP1−18 and PduP cannot be differentiated but we contend that they act in a similar manner. Further, perturbation of the luminal cargo does not influence the cross-links captured among the protein shell as cross-links between PduB138-PduA55 and PduA55-PduJ54 are maintained throughout all datasets. From this, we speculate that the shell may scaffold on, but assemble independently of, the inner core.

The 161 cargo-cargo cross-links can be sub-divided into those directly between EPs-fused cargo (cargoEP-cargoEP), between an EP containing cargo protein and another cargo protein (cargoEP-cargo), or between two non-EP containing cargo proteins (cargo-cargo) (Figure 4d). From these cross-links, we looked at those that directly included the EPs of PduDELP and took an inventory of whether they cross-linked to another EP, a non-EP portion of a cargo protein, or a shell protein (Figure 4e). We find that EPs form cross-links to other EPs but also mainly to other EP-containing cargo proteins. Only three cross-links between the shell (PduB, specifically) and EPs were found and are distributed evenly among PduDEL. From this, we speculate that EPs mainly drive cargo-cargo interactions as opposed to cargo-shell interactions.
The Convex Face of the Shell Protein PduA Interacts with Inner Cargo

Understanding the orientation of the proteins that comprise the outer shell and their interactions with the enzymatic core will be crucial for any future efforts at redesigning BMC. We found 13 cross-links between shell and cargo components. A majority of these cross-links involved the convex face of the shell proteins (Figure 5a). These links were captured between the cargo proteins PduDELM (Figure 5b) and the major shell components PduABJ (Figure 5c). While PduAJ formed links to only PduD170 (red circles, Figures 5b, c), PduB was captured in cross-links to PduDELM, including links between the EPs of PduDEL directly to the convex surface of PduB263 (Figure 5c). This revealed that the convex face of the protein shell faces inward, while the concave face points towards the cytosol. Further, it may suggest that PduB acts as a potential interaction hub between the shell and cargo. However, we are not able to confirm from these data alone whether EPs are specifically responsible for cargo-shell interactions.
The Terminal Extensions of Shell Proteins Follow Sequence-Dependent Rules

A total of 56 cross-links were identified among the protein shell (Figure 6a). These cross-links are sub-divided based on which face of the shell the cross-links were located. The links designated as “other” corresponded to the N- or C-terminal extensions of PduB and PduK, respectively, which have not yet been structurally resolved. It has been suggested that the extension on PduB interacts with cargo and therefore lies luminally, but the location of PduK’s extension has been unknown. Herein, our data revealed cross-links between the N-terminus of PduB and the convex faces of PduAJ (Figure 6b). Moreover, we observed a cross-link between the C-terminus of PduK with the concave faces of PduAJT (Figure 6b). Together, these data confirm that the PduB extension faces inward, where it can in theory interact with cargo, and suggest that the PduK extension faces outward.

Given that our data already established the orientation of the protein shell based on the positions of cargo cross-links, we sought to apply hydroxyl-radical footprinting to further confirm the shell orientation and the placement of the terminal extensions on PduBK (Figure 6c). In this experiment, we measured the oxidation of surface-exposed amino acids using hydroxyl radical generation via the Fenton reaction and determined the percent oxidation using mass spectrometry. Peptides that had the most change (>10%) were deemed exposed. Using PduJ as a case study (due to excellent sequence coverage), our footprinting results showed that the concave-presenting residues on PduJ (M1, L79, P79, and H80; black residues, Figure 6c) exhibited the most oxidation change and therefore are oriented outwardly. In contrast, our data provide additional support that the N-terminal extension of PduB is likely to face toward the BMC lumen.

PduA also has a short C-terminal tail that has been suggested to interact with cargo EPs. We identified unanticipated cross-links between residues in this region (PduA86 and PduA90) to PduJ (Figure 6d). When high-resolution structures of PduA and PduJ are manually placed adjacent to one another, these residues are further apart than the cross-linker would allow (Figure 6d). We also observed cross-links between PduA90, which is on the concave face, to PduA12, which is on the convex face. From these observations we speculate that the short C-terminus of PduA (and perhaps PduJ) might be disordered or flexible. Support for this also comes from recent molecular dynamics analyses of the C-terminal tail of CcmK2, a homolog of PduA, which showed that it exists in a disordered, flexible state. Together, these data suggest BMC-H termini exist predominantly on the outside of the compartment and may play a role in shell-shell interactions. However, it is not yet clear from our data how this C-terminal extension affects cargo EPs. Further investigations of shell protein extensions and their associated linker sequences are warranted.
PduA and PduJ interact with Discrete Edges of the Trimeric Shell Protein PduB

The precise organization of the Pdu BMC protein shell has continued to elude researchers for decades. Key progress has been achieved through analyses of synthetic derivatives of BMCs, such as the Hoch BMC, for which empty shells were analyzed by high-resolution structural approaches. Therefore, we analyzed our cross-links for insights into shell protein patterns. We captured cross-links suggesting that PduB accommodates two sets of interactions. As a trimer, the way PduB domains assemble into a pseudo-hexameric structure creates two distinct edges. When assessing the cross-links between the shell proteins PduA and PduJ to PduB, it became apparent that certain cross-links can only be explained by PduA and PduJ interacting with specific edges (deemed edge A and B) of PduB (Figure 6e).

PduB146 and PduB252 occupy the same positions on the two different BMC domain repeats, yet PduA could only cross-link to PduB146 on the first domain (edge B) and PduJ was only found to cross-link to PduB252 in the second domain (edge A, Figure 6e). Further, PduJ can cross-link to the N-terminus of PduB, which is presumably along the same edge as PduB252. Also, PduA0 (i.e., the free amine at the N-terminus) formed a cross-link to PduB177 on edge B. Both PduA and PduJ share a cross-link to PduB138, which at a vertex in the hexagonal structure of PduB, is accessible from both edges. From our aggregate data, we speculate a model where PduAJ occupy alternating positions around the PduB trimer (Figure 6e). Given the stoichiometries of PduABJ, it is easy to imagine this cyclical arrangement as the fundamental unit of the BMC that makes up the bulk of each facet along the polyhedron (Figure 7a).
DISCUSSION

In this study, we leverage chemical tools to explore the dynamics and protein-protein interactions that form native Pdu BMCs. These assays can be implemented on any purifiable BMC, whether natural or synthetic. Further, our chemical labeling and cross-linking experiments take advantage of the apparent heterogeneity of BMCs that can complicate other structural methods. The list of chemical tools used here is far from exhaustive; we anticipate many more imaginative permutations of these experiments being used on both native and synthetic systems to derivatize BMCs for new functionalities and applications.

Our data show that the Pdu BMC is more permeable than expected. They demonstrate that some proteins within the shell layer can be exchanged with free shell proteins, suggesting that the shell layer may reach dynamic equilibrium with cytoplasmic proteins. At first glance, this may appear to contradict the assumption that a rigid shell is needed to sequester the toxic metabolite intermediates located within. However, we speculate that the shell layer can still act as a diffusion limiting barrier even if it is dynamic. It is tempting to speculate that the overall size and complexity of the Pdu BMC might influence dynamics within its shell layer while also being influenced by the cellular function(s) of the BMC or BMC-like entity. For example, carboxysomes may exhibit more rigidity in their shell layer in order to limit oxygen access to the inner lumen. For these and other reasons, the integrity of the shell layer is likely to greatly influence the biogenesis, maintenance and deconstruction of BMCs. Therefore, much more work is needed to address this important topic, including development of experimental approaches that quantitatively measure dynamics of shell layer proteins. These approaches will also help determine if shell proteins exchange with cytoplasmic proteins, as we hypothesize herein, or if they can be exchanged due to general damage in the shell layer of purified compartments.

Decades of research into BMCs have attempted to delineate the interactome of these complex entities. Here, we used XL-MS to globally capture interaction data in native BMCs in vitro. We initially predicted that shell-cargo cross-links would dominate our data because we assumed that interactions between EPs and the protein shell would be commonplace and located at the easily accessible shell-lumen interface. However, while cross-links that include EPs account for nearly a third of the cross-links we identified, only three were to shell proteins. Therefore, our findings suggest that EPs might be more critical for cargo-cargo interactions than for shell-cargo interactions.

It is important to note that none of the Pdu EP-containing proteins present as a monomer. PduP is likely a tetramer, PduL is at least a dimer, interestingly influenced by the presence of its EP,, and PduCDE exists as a dimer of trimers. The widespread interactions we captured between these proteins, coupled to their mismatched multivalency, invites comparisons to the ‘stickers and spacers’ model used to describe biomolecular condensation (Figure 7b). From this, we speculate that the inner lumen might be a disordered biomolecular condensate that is constrained by the protein shell (Figure 7b). This may suggest that efforts to synthetically manipulate BMCs, such as incorporation of designer cargo, may need to consider using multiple EP fusions with mismatched valencies. This may encourage heterotypic interactions over the homotypic interactions that led to aggregation observed in cargo protein purification efforts.

From our total data, we speculate that the Pdu BMC is a plastic system governed by a multitude of multivalent interactions. Our data is consistent with a model where the inner cargo first undergoes LLPS to form an EP-driven pro-metabolosome, prior to or concomitant with shell envelopment. A prediction of this overall model is that if the cargo undergoes LLPS, it should exhibit a strong reliance on mismatched valencies of protein-protein interaction points, such as EPs. Given this, it is interesting that the BMCs containing GFPP1−18 resulted in less than half the yield per purification preparation, compared to wild-type BMCs. Perhaps the monomeric state of GFPP1−18 resulted in dead-end network extensions, thereby perturbing the proper assembly pathway.

Since there are still unresolved questions about the stoichiometry and spatial arrangement of shell proteins, we examined our data closely for any insights. We confirm that native BMC shells have the same topology as synthetic, empty shells (concave out), thereby reaffirming the modularity of these systems. Our analysis also suggested that the Pdu BMC shell may employ a fundamental repeating unit, consisting of a cyclical arrangement of BMC-H proteins around BMC-T types (Figure 7a). Here, BMC-T proteins punctuate the facets and are spaced by BMC-H types. Our data specifically implicates PduA and PduJ in alternating positions around PduB (Figure 7a). Overall, our shell model is like the structural model presented for the Hoch BMC, wherein the center of each facet is occupied by a BMC-T protein surrounded by BMC-H. In contrast, our model differs from an alternate arrangement that was proposed from measurements of stoichiometric data, which proposes that PduB occupy the edges of each face.

Finally, our data suggest that the trimeric protein PduB may act as a hub for shell-cargo interactions. This is consistent with prior studies that showed that perturbation of the N-terminus of PduB leads to aberrant cargo packaging. If true, we speculate that the N-terminus of PduB may act as a cognate EP to anchor/seed shell formation around the inner cargo. The distributive arrangement of BMC-T proteins that we propose (Figure 7a) and the need for two isoforms of PduB are consistent with this. Recent modeling suggested that increased interactions between shell and cargo can lead to premature cargo encapsulation and aberrant structures. In this context, the combination of PduB and PduB’ interactions with the inner cargo might therefore be needed to permit proper condensate maturation prior to shell envelopment. Perhaps the protein shell can be viewed as a stabilizing factor that scaffolds on the inner core while introducing a more-or-less predestined curvature and size. Here, in this model, the Pdu BMC may form through biomolecular condensation but once assembled it exists actively as a shell-stabilized entity. We consider our data to be consistent with this overall model.

In conclusion, this study highlights a series of methods that can yield structural information for large, heterogenous complexes where traditional structural approaches struggle. Through a small battery of chemical probes, we find that the Pdu BMC is a complex and dynamic system. It is worth noting that many more chemical probes are commercially available; therefore, the approaches used herein can be varied in many ways to interrogate assembly of BMC or to improve the development of BMC as drug delivery vehicles. In total, our data provide key insight into the native assembly of a bacterial BMC and suggest features that will need to be considered for future synthetic designs.

METHOD DETAILS
Probe and Cross-Linker Preparation

Cross-linkers and fluorescent probes used in this study were prepared as smaller single-use aliquots to extend their utility and cut down on costs. AF488, AF532 and AF680 were resuspended in 1:9 (v/v) water:acetonitrile and aliquoted into 40 nmol portions in 1.5 mL microcentrifuge tubes. Aliquots were then vacuum evaporated, sealed, and stored at −20°C under desiccant in the dark. The cross-linkers BS(PEG)5 and sulfo-EGS were prepared similarly but resuspended in anhydrous, degassed DMSO in a dehumidified anaerobic hood prior to being aliquoted. Aliquots were then sealed and stored at −20°C under desiccant. DSBU and BS3 were purchased in commercially available single-use aliquots and resuspended in anhydrous DMSO prior to use. AF532, AF680, and BS(PEG)5, and sulfo-EGS were found to be highly reactive >4 months after being prepared as described.
BMC Purification from a Heterologous Host

BMCs were purified in a similar way to previously described methods. Briefly, A single colony of R995 + PduST was used to inoculate 100 mL of 2xYT supplemented with kanamycin and 0.5% 1,2-propanediol and grown overnight at 37°C for ~16 hours. The next day, the culture was pelleted and resuspend in 20 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 200 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 5 mM β-mercaptoethanol (βME), 0.5 mM EDTA, 0.5 mg/mL lysozyme, 0.5 mM PMSF and 50% B-PER (Thermo) (v/v) and gently rocked at RT for 25 minutes and then placed on ice for 5 minutes. gDNA was then cleared by 2×1s pulses in a sonicator. Insoluble matter was pelleted for 20 minutes at 13000xg, 4°C. BMCs were pelleted at 17500xg, 4°C for 40 minutes. Pelleted BMCs were then resuspended in labeling buffer (20 mM phosphate pH 7.4, 50 mM KCl, 5 mM MgCl2) and pelleted again for 20 minutes. The final BMC pellet was resuspend in 1 mL of labeling buffer and stored at 4°C for less than two weeks. BMCs were quantified via Bradford Assay.

BMCs containing GFPP1−18 were sourced from the same strain containing EYK054. Growth and purification proceeded as above, except growth media volume was doubled and also contained 0.005% L-arabinose to induce GFPP1−18 expression.
Microscopy

For in vivo imaging of BMCs, R995 + PduST co-transformed with EYK054 were grown overnight then diluted 1:100 in fresh 2xYT supplemented with 0.5% 1,2-propanediol and 0.005% L-arabinose. Cultures were grown for 5.5 hours at 37°C before being pelleted and resuspended in 1x PBS. Samples were then spotted onto an agarose pad and imaged on a Zeiss Axio Observer Z1.

For in vitro imaging of purified, fluorescently tagged BMCs, samples were purified and fluorescently labeled with AF488 as described for 30 minutes on ice. After labeling, BMCs were fixed in 2% paraformaldehyde for 30 minutes on ice then pelleted at 20000xg for 15 minutes at 4°C. Supernatant was removed and the BMC pellet was resuspended in labeling buffer. A single pelleting round removed nearly all unincorporated dye. Prepared BMCs were imaging directly on a non-absorbent 1.5 glass coverslip at 63x magnification with oil by a Ziess LSM 980 Airyscan.

For TEM, BMC samples were diluted in labeling buffer to 0.1 mg/mL and 5 μL applied to a formvar coated copper grid, 200 mesh (FCF200-CU, Electron Microscope Sciences). Samples were air dried for 15 minutes and excess was wicked off. Salt was removed by 3×5 μL additions of deionized water before staining with 3 μL of 2% uranyl acetate for 10 seconds. Samples were imaged using a JEOL 100CXII electron microscope.
Labeling Assays

For the 1-dye assay, purified BMCs are diluted to 1.0 mg/mL in labeling buffer and split into a denatured control and native sample. The denatured control has SDS added to 0.5% and is heated at 95°C for 5 minutes. Both samples were equilibrated to room temperature before an aliquot of AF532 was added to 125 μM in both samples. Aliquots were taken from each at the designated timepoints and quenched by adding βME to 5 mM. Aliquots were taken and dialyzed against deionized water to remove excess AF532. Samples were separated via standard SDS-PAGE and resulting bands were analyzed in ImageJ.

For the 2-dye assay, purified BMCs are diluted to 1.0 mg/mL as above. AF532 was added to 125 μM and BMCs were labeled for 15 minutes at RT before being quenched as above. Samples were then dialyzed against 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 0.5% SDS to remove excess βME before being heated at 95°C for 5 minutes. AF680 was then added to 250 μM and samples were labeled for 90 minutes at RT and quenched as above. Samples were then alkylated with 20 mM 2-chloroacetamide for 1 hour at RT protected from light. AF680 was found not to dialyze well so samples were subject to buffer exchange columns to remove excess AF680 and 2-chloroacetamide. Samples were equilibrated into 2D-PAGE rehydration buffer (8 M urea, 0.25% CHAPS, 0.5% 3–10 NL ampholytes, 20 mM DTT, trace bromophenol blue) for 2D separation.

For the biotin pulldown, purified BMCs were diluted to 1.0 mg/mL in labeling buffer and equilibrated to RT. Probe A was added to 125 μM and BMCs were labeled for 5 minutes. Reactions were quenched by addition of βME to 625 μM followed by denaturation by adding SDS to 0.5% and heating. Once cooled to RT, probe B was added to 1 mM and reacted for 30 minutes. Samples were then dialyzed overnight into pulldown buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 50 mM NaCl). Dialyzed, labeled samples were incubated with equilibrated NeutrAvidin™ Agarose (Pierce) for 15 minutes on ice. Supernatant was collected and the beads were washed once with pulldown buffer. Bound proteins were eluted by mixing the beads with 1x standard SDS-PAGE sample buffer + 2 mg/mL D-biotin and heating for 1 minute at 98°C.
2D-Electrophoresis and Peptide Mass Fingerprinting

The ZOOM® IPGRunner™ System (Invitrogen) was used for 2D separation. Briefly, samples were diluted into rehydration buffer and approximately 15 μg of protein sample was loaded onto a pH 3–10 NL IPG strip and equilibrated for 6 hours at RT. Samples then underwent isoelectric focusing overnight with stepwise increases in voltage and held for final focusing overnight (16 hours, 2000 V). After focusing, strips were retrieved and incubated in 1x NuPAGE LDS Buffer supplemented with 5 mM DTT for 5 minutes prior to separation via 4–20% PAGE. Gels were fluorescently scanned prior to silver staining/destaining of excised spots with SilverQuest™ Silver Staining Kit (Invitrogen).

Excised gel spots were washed once in 25 mM NH4HCO3 before being dehydrated in acetonitrile for 15 minutes at RT. Alkylation was skipped since samples had already been alkylated. Dehydrated gel pieces were swelled in 50 μL of 20 ng/μL of Trypsin/LysC (Promega) in 25 mM NH4HCO3 for 30 minutes at 37°C then excess supernatant was removed and digestion was allowed to continue overnight at 37°C. After digestion, peptides were desalted and extracted using C18 tips (Pierce) and eluted in 20 μL of 0.1% TFA, 50% acetonitrile. Samples were analyzed in a Bruker Autoflex Speed MALDI-TOF in DHB/CHCA matrices in linear mode. Peaks were analyzed in MS-Fit using the NCBI non-redundant database for Salmonella species. A mass tolerance of ±2 Da was used and a minimum of 3 peptides was needed for a match.
Dynamic Light Scattering

Labeling samples were prepared as described in other sections. BMC samples were diluted to 0.1 mg/mL in labeling buffer and equilibrated to room temperature immediately prior to measurement. Light scattering measurements were performed on a Nanobrook Omni Particle Sizer with 90° scatter and analyzed using the CONTIN model. Three biological replicates were measured twice for a total of 6 measurements per condition. Each scan was performed for 90 seconds at RT.
PduA Purification, Labeling, and BMC Pull Down Assay

The plasmid encoding PduA S93C was sub-cloned via Gibson assembly, sequence confirmed, and transformed into T7 Express to create strain DT074. Overnights were used to inoculate 500 mL of 2xYT supplemented with antibiotic to an OD600 and grown at 37°C to an OD600 of 0.6–0.8. PduA was expressed by addition of IPTG to 0.5 mM and incubated at 30°C for 4.5 hours. Cultures were then pelleted, frozen/thawed, and resuspended in Buffer A (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0, 1 M NaCl, 5 mM DTT, and 10 mM imidazole) and lysed via sonication. Insoluble matter was pelleted for 20 minutes at 13000xg, 4°C. The soluble lysate was then equilibrated with 1 mL of equilibrated IMAC resin for 30 minutes at 4°C before being applied to a gravity column. Flowthrough was drained off and the beads were washed with 5 mL of Buffer A, 5 mM of Buffer B (Buffer A + 35 mM imidazole) and PduA S93C was eluted in 5 mL Buffer C (Buffer A + 250 mM imidazole). Eluted protein was dialyzed against 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 100 mM NaCl, 10% glycerol. Purified PduA were labeling with AF532 at a ratio of 1:2 AF532:PduA for 2 hours on ice. Purified and labeling proteins were stored at −20°C for later use.

After labeling, PduA* was incubated either with or without 1.0 mg/mL Pdu BMCs for 30 minutes on ice at a concentration of 50 μM in BMC labeling buffer. After incubation, samples were pelleted at 20000xg for 15 minutes. Supernatant was removed and BMC pellets were resuspended in labeling buffer and samples were separated on SDS-PAGE.
BMC Crosslinking

BMCs are diluted to 1.0 mg/mL in labeling buffer and equilibrated to room temperature. Regardless of crosslinker used, all were equilibrated to room temperature then added immediately such that the final concentration of DMSO never exceeds 2%. Crosslinking reactions proceeded for 45 minutes at room temperature with gentle rocking. Quenching was performed by adding Tris-HCl pH 8.0 to a final concentration of 5 mM.
Mass Spectrometry

Cross-linked samples were acetone precipitated and resuspended in 5% SDS prior to reduction in 200 mM DTT for 1 hour at 57°C. Samples were then alkylated with 500 mM iodoacetamide for 45 minutes in the dark at RT and quenched by addition of 200 mM DTT. 50 μg of sample were then cleaned and digested in S-Trap™ Micro Spin Columns (ProtoFi) according to manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, samples were acidified with 5 μL of 12% phosphoric acid and proteins precipitated by six times dilution with S-Trap buffer (100 mM TEAB in 90% MeOH, pH = 7.1) and captured on porous micro S-Trap spin column beads. S-Trap columns were washed three times with 150 μL of S-Trap buffer followed by digestion in 20 μL of 50 mM ammonium bicarbonate solution containing 1 μg of trypsin (Promega). Digestions were completed in 1 h at 47°C and peptides were eluted, dried, and resuspended in 0.5% acetic acid. Digested peptides were eluted in 40% acetonitrile, 0.5% acetic acid followed by 80% acetonitrile, 0.5% acetic acid, dried, and resuspended in 0.5% acetic acid and stored at −80°C until analysis.

For DSBU and BS(PEG)5 samples, approximately 7 μg of the sample was analyzed. Samples were separated online using an EASY-nLC 1200 (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and with a flow rate of 200 nL/min and eluted in a gradient of 2–80% acetonitrile, 0.5% acetic acid over 220 minutes into an Orbitrap Fusion Eclipse spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Full MS spectra were acquired with a resolution of 60,000 (at m/z 200), AGC target of 4×105, max. ion time of 50 ms, and scan range of 400–2000 m/z. MS2 spectra were collected with a cycle time of 3 seconds in the ion trap using rapid scan with a resolution of 30,000, AGC target of 5e4, max. ion time of 70 ms, one microscan, 1.6 m/z isolation window and HCD using stepped 15, 30, and 45% normalized collision energy and CID of 25%. A fragment mass filter for 85.0527 and 111.032 to select crosslinked peptides for MS3. MS3 spectra were collected with IT set to rapid, AGC of 2e4 max. ion time of 70 ms, one microscan, 2.5 m/z isolation window, and HCD of 27%. MS/MS spectra were analyzed using Sequest and XlinkX within Proteome Discoverer 2.53. A mass tolerance of 10 Da was set for MS1 and 0.5 Da for MS2. Xlinks were searched using non-cleavable acquisition strategy, 1.5 signal to noise ratio, FDR of 0.01, and variable Xlink modification on lysine of +138.068 for DSS and BS3 and +302.137 for BS(PEG)5. The following modifications were allowed: fixed: carbamidomethyl on cysteines (+57.021); variable: DSS/BS3 Tris on Lysine (+259.142), DSS/BS3 hydrolyzed on lysine (+156.079), BS(PEG)5 Tris on lysine (+424.218), BS(PEG)5 hydrolyzed on lysine (+320.147), oxidation on methionine (+15.995) and deamidated on asparagine (+0.984). While the cross-linker BS3 was used, it led to the identification of redundant cross-links reported within other datasets. The mass spectrometry raw files acquired at the Proteomics Laboratory at NYU are accessible at https://massive.ucsd.edu under accession MassIVE MSV000088460. A list of all unique cross-links identified can be found in Data S1.

DSSO treated samples were run on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer equipped with a Thermo Ultimate 3500 UPLC and FAIMS unit operating under 3 different CVs (−50, −60, and −75). Chromatography was performed using Mass Spec Grade reagents (H2O and 0.1% formic acid for buffer A and 95% acetonitrile with 5% H2O 0.1% formic acid for buffer B). A 75 cm Thermo Fisher Easy-Spray column was utilized for separation. A 200-minute gradient was utilized for separation at a 0.3 μL/min flow rate (0 min 5%B, 10 min 10%B, 150 min 70%B, 158 min 80%B, 161 min 90%B, 171 min 90%B, 172min 5%B, 200 min 5%B). MS1 was collected in the orbitrap at a resolution of 60,000 scanning from 375–1500 m/z with standard AGC target and MIPS active. An intensity threshold of 2.04e4 was utilized along with charge state inclusion between 2 and 8. Dynamic exclusion was held to 45 min with a mass tolerance of 20 ppm. For stepped collision energy MS2 acquisition, HCD assisted collision energies of 25% and 30% were used. MS2 scans were collected in the orbitrap at a resolution of 30,000. A normalized AGC target of 200% was used with a maximum injection time of 70 ms. For the MS2/MS3 acquisition, a fixed CID collision energy of 25% was used and MS2 scans were collected in the orbitrap at 30,000 resolution at standard AGC target and 70 ms max injection time. MIPS was then used and a targeted mass difference of 31.9721 m/z was used for the DSSO crosslinker. A charge state filter of 2–6 was utilized followed by precursor ion exclusion with a 50 ppm mass width. Two MS3 scans were performed in the ion trap operating under rapid scan mode using a fixed CID energy of 35%. An AGC target of 200% was used with a maximum injection time of 120 ms. For the MS2/MS2/MS3 acquisition, a fixed CID collision energy of 25% was used and MS2 scans were collected in the orbitrap at a resolution of 50,000. MIPS was then used and a targeted mass difference of 31.9721 m/z was used for the DSSO crosslinker. A secondary MS2 scan was collected post-targeted mass identification in the orbitrap at a resolution of 30,000 utilizing ETD fragmentation. A defined mass range of 150–2000 m/z was used with a maximum injection time of 100 ms. For the MS3 scan, charge state filtering was performed post targeted mass identification to include charge states between 2 and 6 followed by precursor ion exclusion with a 50 ppm mass width. Two scans were obtained in the ion trap operating under rapid scan rate with fixed CID collision energy of 35%. An AGC target of 200% was used with a maximum injection time of 120 ms. All data was processed in Thermo Proteome Discoverer 2.5 using the Xlinkx node for cross-link identification. The mass spectrometry proteomics data have been deposited to the ProteomeXchange Consortium via the PRIDE partner repository with the dataset identifier PXD029675. Data reported here all have an Xlinkx score greater than 30. A list of all unique cross-links identified can be found in Data S1.
Hydroxyl Radical Footprinting

Aliquots of 45 μL of 5 μM samples in 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8.0 buffer were used for each reaction condition in triplicates. Samples were reacted with 15 mM, 7.5 mM, 3.25 mM, and 0 mM of iron(II) sulfate heptahydrate and hydrogen peroxide at 2 fold excess, respectively, for 2 minutes. The reaction was quenched with 50 μL of 0.1 ng/μL catalase, 68 μM thiourea, and 34 μM methioninamide. The samples were subsequently incubated with 50 μM Poros Beads for 2 hours at 4°C. The beads were then loaded onto C4 ZipTips, washed 3 times with 0.1% TFA, 3 times with 0.5% acetic acid and eluted with 40% acetonitrile followed by 80% acetonitrile in 0.5% acetic acid and subsequently concentrated in a SpeedVac concentrator. The model Pdu BMC used in this study.

(A) A schematic of the Pdu BMC from S. enterica Typhimurium LT2 used in this study. (B) Pdu BMCs visualized by fluorescence microscopy in vivo in E. coli expressing the S. enterica Pdu BMC operon in tandem with a GFP containing an EP. BMCs appear as green foci distributed throughout the cell. Scale bar, 5 μm. (C) Negative stain transmission electron micrographs of purified Pdu BMCs. BMCs appear as protein globules and are denoted by arrows. Scale bar, 500 nm. (D) SDS-PAGE of S. enterica Pdu BMCs expressed and purified from a heterologous host. Lyso., lysozyme.
Chemical probing of Pdu BMCs.

(A) In vitro time course labeling of BMCs with the cysteine reactive fluorophore AF532. 70* refers to the 60-minute timepoint being denatured and labeling for another 10 minutes. Shell proteins are bolded. (B) Quantification of time course labeling. Bands are quantified as a fraction of their fluorescent contribution per timepoint (band/lane). Error bars are S.D. of three experimental replicates. (C) A schematic of a dual-labeling workflow. (D) 1D and 2D-PAGE of a dual-labeled BMC sample. Identification of individual spots can be found in supplemental Figure S2. (E) Quantification of fluorescent intensity of specific zones from panel D. Red and green fluorescence is quantified separately, and the ratio of their intensities is plotted. A representative protein identified by peptide mass fingerprinting per zone is listed. (F) SDS-PAGE of dual-probing relying on biotinylation as the basis for separation. Lane A, elution of samples labeled with biotin then maleimide; Lane B, elution of samples labeled with maleimide then biotin. Green boxes correspond to shell protein bands, red boxes correspond to prominent cargo proteins. (G) Pdu BMCs fluorescently labeled with fluorophores are directly imaged with confocal microscopy in a labeling-specific manner. Scale bar, 5 μm.
BMCs display a tolerance and dynamic permeability towards bioconjugation.

(A) BMCs cross-linked with the cleavable cross-linker sulfo-EGS. Dashed box notes cross-linked species. (B and C) Permeability assay where BMCs were cross-linked with sulfo-EGS then labeled as in Figure 2a. The intensity ratio of a distinct shell protein band to specified cargo components is plotted. Error bars are S.D. of three experimental replicates. (C) Fluorophore labeled PduA (PduA*) colocalization to native Pdu BMCs in vitro. Dashed inset was fluorescently scanned, below. (E) Dynamic light scattering measurements of purified BMCs. BMC samples examined were either native or incubated with DMSO (2%) as a buffer control, thiol reactive AF532 (125 μM), and amine reactive BS3 (5 mM). (B) Polydispersity from DLS measurements. Asterisk indicates samples that were significantly different (p > 0.05).
A summary of protein-protein interactions involving cargo proteins.

(A) A pie chart is shown of the unique cross-links that were identified between cargo proteins. A full list of unique crosslinks is included in Data S1. (B) A protein-protein interactome heat map describing the cross-links that were identified. Cross-links are colored according to the number of unique cross-links identified between proteins. Proteins are scaled by their primary sequence length, with shell proteins shown as hexagons/pentagons and cargo proteins as circles. Blue cargo proteins feature encapsulation peptides (EP). Asterisks denote cross-linking partners of an EP-tagged GFP protein, GFPP1–18. (C) SDS-PAGE analysis of a BMC sample shows GFPP1−18 is part of the BMC when expressed (+) in tandem. Red arrow denotes PduP, black arrows denote GFPP1–18. (D) Summary of the cargo-cargo cross-links captured. EP-containing proteins, cargoEP. (E) An enumeration of the cross-links to EPs. Cross-links to EPs are tabulated as occurring directly to another EP, to the main body of another cargo protein, or to shell proteins.
The convex face of shell proteins faces internally.

(A) A pie chart summary of the sides of shell proteins that cargo proteins cross-linked to. “Other” refers to the N-terminus of PduB. (B) Depiction of the cargo proteins that cross-linked to shell proteins. Blue proteins contain encapsulation peptides (EPs). The inner circles denote specific amino acids with those on EPs having an asterisk. (C) A depiction of where cargo cross-links occurred on the shell proteins PduJ (5D6V, cyan), PduA (3NGK, green), and PduB (homology model of 4FAY, magenta). Circles show where cross-links occurred and are color coded according to panel (B). The N-terminus of PduB is shown as a gray circle and is assumed to be on the convex face.
Cross-links among shell proteins.

(A) A summary of the shell-shell cross-links classified by which surfaces cross-link to one another. “Other” cross-links denote those to the N- and C-termini of PduB and PduK, respectively. (B) An account of which surface of other shell proteins that the N- and C-termini of PduB and PduK, respectively, link to. (C) Hydroxyl-radical footprinting of the shell protein PduJ (shown, 5D6V). The oxidation state of specific peptides was quantified (right) as a function of oxidant added. Those with the greatest response (orange) are deemed surface exposed. Specific residues (black, left) carry most of the oxidation change. (D) The C-terminal tails (shaded gray) of PduA (3NGK, green) and PduJ (5D6V, cyan) make contacts too far to be explained by the known crystal forms and cross-link spacer length. PDB files were visualized, distances measured, and manually oriented in Pymol. (E) The BMC-T protein PduB (homology model of 4FAY, magenta) forms edge-dependent cross-links to PduA and PduJ.
Proposed model of the Pdu BMC.

The sum of the cross-linking data allows us to propose models for the organization of the protein shell and enzymatic cargo. (A) Model of the protein shell. Cross-linking data suggests PduB is surrounded by an alternating pattern of PduA and PduJ and may represent a fundamental pattern in the protein shell. (B) Model of the multivalent, EP-driven interactions present within the BMC lumen among cargo proteins. EP-containing proteins form an extended, promiscuous interaction network while others engage in piggybacking interactions. The shell proteins are oriented concave out, leaving the convex face to support luminal interactions with cargo, potentially with EPs.
